lines: A table gets split up by customer, because that sounds like the fast way to look someone up.
A year later, the job that totals up each night's revenue is crawling, and a request to erase one customer turns into rewriting nearly everything.
Two completely different-looking problems. Do they actually share one single cause?
Worth reasoning through before the reveal settles it.
A bigger machine could probably push through the slow nightly job eventually. And the erasure request looks, on its face, like an entirely separate kind of problem.
Or is there one earlier decision that actually explains both of these at once?
answer: Not two problems. One decision, showing up twice.
More machine never fixes a layout that forces scanning nearly everything, no matter how fast that machine is.
And the split that was chosen wasn't picked by asking which question gets asked of this data the most. It was picked because it merely sounded fast.

lines: Before touching layout at all, one earlier question: which copy of this data is the real one?
Some data is the one and only authoritative record. Other data is simply computed from that record, and could be thrown away and rebuilt at any time.
Knowing which is which decides what actually needs careful backing up, and what doesn't.
Here's the actual fix: find the one question this data gets asked most often, and split the data to match that question.
The nightly job asks for one day at a time. So the data should be split up by day, not by who it belongs to.
The split should follow the question being asked, not whatever sounded intuitive at the time.
One format choice sits above all of this, and it isn't reinvented fresh for every single dataset either.
Several formats can all represent the same data. What actually tells them apart is how well each one plays with other tools, and the catalog each one needs.
That's the one cost that actually decides between them — and once a format is picked, the physical layout simply follows from it.
Draw that same nightly question as a beam crossing straight through both ways of splitting the data.
Split by owner, the beam clips nearly every single piece. Split by day, the beam only needs a handful of pieces, and almost everything else gets skipped entirely, untouched.
Not all data deserves the same shelf. Recent data sits somewhere fast and costly. Older data moves somewhere cheaper. The oldest gets tucked away in deep storage.
Each shelf carries its own clock. A shelf isn't just a price tag — it's a promise about exactly how long that data is allowed to sit there.
That clock isn't just good engineering practice, either.
Privacy law itself says personal information can't be kept around, in a form that identifies someone, for any longer than its actual purpose requires.
The clock on every shelf is answering a real requirement, not just following a tidy convention.
One more to reason through: someone asks to be erased. Under the day-based split, do all of their records sit together in one place?
Or could their history be scattered across every single day they ever showed up on?
answer: Scattered. Splitting by day groups records by day, never by who they belong to.
So one person's whole history ends up spread across however many days they were ever active.
Plan for erasure from the very start, and it costs picking the right grouping up front. Bolt it on afterward, and it costs rewriting every shelf that history ever touched.

lines: Settle which copy is the real one before anything else gets decided.
Let the question actually being asked choose how the data gets split — never instinct.
Give every shelf its own clock, backed by an actual requirement, not a guess.
And plan for erasure from day one, or pay for skipping that later, in a full rewrite.
One more, to use this for real: a second dataset, of session records, mostly gets asked one different question — find one specific session, instantly, by its own id.
What does that change about how this one should be split up, and does the same erasure headache still show up?
answer: Split this one by session id instead, since that's the question actually being asked of it.
And yes, the same risk can still show up — if one person's many sessions end up scattered across many separate groupings rather than kept together.
A quick lookup helps find one row fast, but it never decides whether a split keeps one person's data together or scatters it. That's still a separate question, worth asking every time.
